text.p: Serbian authorities in the troubled province of Kosovo charged 21 ethnic Albanians on Monday with belonging to a "hostile terrorist association", the Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said.
It said 18 of the accused were in custody and three at large. No trial date has been set.

The prosecutor's office in the provincial capital Pristina said the 21 joined the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army in early 1992 and remained active throughout the Albanian-majority region until the beginning of 1997.
The group was charged with a number of premeditated murders and attempted murders in several dozen attacks on policemen, police stations, refugee buildings and other locations, Tanjug said.
It said the attacks in the impoverished southern province "inflicted a great deal of material damage".

The prosecutor's office said they planned and carried out violence against the Yugoslav constitutional system and security with the aim of having Kosovo secede and form a separate state to be subsequently united with Albania.

It said they armed themselves with a large quality of weapons - automatic rifles, sniper rifles, handguns, ammunition, hand grenades, various explosive devices, rifle-launched grenades and other ordnance.
Kosovo, where ethnic Albanians outnumber Serbs nine to one, is widely regarded as a political powder keg which, if ignited, could wreck international peace efforts in the Balkans.

Some 30 people, both Serbs and Albanians, have been killed over the past year in guerrilla violence. Serbian police cracked down in the province in January, arresting some 70 people in a sweep after the guerrilla wave.
This is the third trial this year of ethnic Albanians charged with terrorism in which some 30 of the defendants have been sentenced from one to 20 years in prison.

The United States has made an improvement in Serbia's treatment of Kosovo one of its conditions for lifting remaining sanctions in force against federal Yugoslavia, comprised of Serbia and the tiny republic of Montenegro.
Serbia revoked Kosovo's autonomy in 1989, claiming its Albanian population wanted to secede and join neighbouring Albania.
The Kosovo Albanians have boycotted Serbian institutions since then but they have been warned by the United States that secession is not an option.
